passages.t: ‘You have kept my eyes from closing’: a sleepless night
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. According to Jeduthun. A Psalm of Asaph” (verse 1). Then: “I cried out to God; I cried aloud to God to hear me” (verse 1).

This is a prayer from a long night, “through the night my outstretched hands did not grow weary; my soul refused to be comforted” (verse 2). He tried to think about God, and it only made things worse: “I remembered You, O God, and I groaned” (verse 3). He cannot sleep, and he cannot find words: “You have kept my eyes from closing; I am too troubled to speak” (verse 4).

He thinks back to better days and remembers the songs he used to sing (verses 5 to 6). Then six hard questions pour out. “Will the Lord spurn us forever and never show His favor again? Is His loving devotion gone forever? Has His promise failed for all time? Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has His anger shut off His compassion?” (verses 7 to 9).
passages.hearers:
Jeduthun was one of the leaders of the temple music in David's day, with Asaph and Heman. His name also heads Psalms 39 and 62. ‘According to Jeduthun’ may mean the psalm was sung by his singers or in his style.

The psalm does not name the trouble. It begins as one person's prayer, ‘I cried out’, but by verse 7 he is asking about ‘us’. His own pain and his people's pain have run together.

Look closely at the six questions. Each one names something God had promised to be. Israel had heard God call himself “compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). The man takes those very words and asks: is that still true? It is not a denial of faith. It is a believer holding God's own words up to him in the dark.

Lifting the hands (verse 2) was the usual way to pray.
passages.later: The psalm's questions are close to those of Job and of Habakkuk, who also argued with God from inside his faith. Jesus himself prayed through a night of anguish in Gethsemane, falling on his face (Matthew 26:39).
passages.hard:
What if, like this man, thinking about God makes you feel worse, not better (verse 3)? The psalm does not pretend that never happens. It shows a believer for whom remembering God, at first, only brought groans. If that is where you are, you are not alone in it, and you are not the first.

If sleepless nights have become your normal, please tell someone you trust: a doctor, a pastor or a friend. Lost sleep and heavy thoughts are worth taking to a doctor, and doing so is not a failure of faith. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks:
Have you had a night like this? You may pray this psalm's questions as your own. They are in the Bible, and they were prayed by a temple singer.

Notice that he did not stop asking. He kept talking to God through the night. The next part of the psalm shows where that led.

passages.t: ‘I will remember Your wonders of old’: footprints in the sea
passages.happening:
Verse 10 is the hinge. He says, “I am grieved that the right hand of the Most High has changed” (verse 10). He names his deepest fear plainly: God's strong hand is no longer working for him.

Then he makes a choice. “I will remember the works of the LORD; yes, I will remember Your wonders of old” (verse 11). He thinks back to the exodus, when God rescued his people from Egypt. “With power You redeemed Your people” (verse 15). The waters saw God and were shaken (verse 16). Thunder and lightning filled the sky (verses 17 to 18).

Then comes one of the most beautiful lines in the Psalms. “Your path led through the sea, Your way through the mighty waters, but Your footprints were not to be found” (verse 19). It ends quietly. “You led Your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
The exodus was the story that made Israel a people. They told it every year at Passover. So when this man runs out of answers, he goes back to the story everyone knew.

Notice what he says about God in the sea: he led them through, but no one saw his footprints. God was there, leading, yet out of sight. That is the answer the psalm gives to the night of verses 1 to 9. It does not say God's hand is easy to see. It says that even at the Red Sea, where God did his greatest rescue, his steps could not be seen.

And notice how the psalm ends. It does not end with the storm. It ends with a shepherd leading a flock, by human hands, the hands of Moses and Aaron.
passages.later:
Habakkuk's prayer uses the same pictures: “The mountains saw You and quaked; torrents of water swept by. The deep roared with its voice and lifted its hands on high” (Habakkuk 3:10).

In the Gospel of Mark, in the dark hours of the night, “Jesus went out to them, walking on the sea” (Mark 6:48). He told the frightened disciples, “Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid” (Mark 6:50).
passages.asks:
When God seems far, what do you remember? This man did not find comfort by thinking about his feelings. He found it by turning to what God had done.

You may not be able to see God's footprints in your life right now. Psalm 77 says that was true even at the Red Sea. Ask God to lead you like a flock, even when you cannot see his steps, and look for the human hands he may be using to do it.
